lesson.title: Data in class: record, chart, decide
lesson.subtitle: From readings to a decision, step by step

video.title: Data in class: record, chart, decide
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Okafor — Grade 8 science teacher (main character)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor’s science room. He holds up a notebook crammed with columns of numbers, proud, then frowns as a pupil from the garden club appears at the door holding a watering can and a drooping tomato plant.
scenes.animation: Notebook pages flutter; quick push-in on Okafor’s frown.
scenes.narration: Two weeks of rain readings! Every morning, my pupils read the gauge. Now the garden club asks, “Should we water today?” And I’m staring at a page of numbers.
scenes.sound: Page flutter; light music bed starts.
scenes.vids: Character: illustrated Grade 8 science teacher, enthusiastic, ink outlines. Show numbers as grey lines, not readable text.

scenes.visual: Paper-grey card. The Darsi mark pops in, then the lesson title and the IoT track chip with its icon.
scenes.animation: Mark scales 0→100% with a small overshoot (≤ 200 ms); title slides up.
scenes.on_screen_text: Data in class: record, chart, decide
scenes.narration: Today: how to record, chart and use data to make a decision.
scenes.vids: Use the Darsi title template (see brand kit). Keep the chip as icon + word.

scenes.visual: A question bubble — a watering can with a question mark — floats over the school garden. Below it, four empty cards appear in a row: a notebook, a bar chart, a magnifying glass, a watering can.
scenes.animation: Bubble pops; the four cards appear 300 ms apart.
scenes.narration: Data is facts we collect to answer a question. Our question: should we water the garden? Readings alone won’t answer it. We need four steps: record, chart, spot the pattern, decide.
scenes.vids: Keep the four cards on screen for 3 seconds at the end.

scenes.visual: The notebook card grows to fill the screen: a neat table with three columns and seven rows. A pencil fills in numbers row by row; one row gets a zero, one gets a short word. A blank box blinks with a question mark.
scenes.animation: Rows fill 300 ms apart; the blank box blinks twice.
scenes.narration: Step one: record. A table with a row for each day, and headings with units — date, time, rain in millimetres. Write zero for a dry day, and “missed” if nobody read the gauge. A blank could mean either.
scenes.vids: Show the column headings as text overlays so they can be translated.

scenes.visual: Clean card on white with the IoT track chip. The table’s numbers rise into bars of matching heights; a side axis with equal tick marks appears, with a small unit tag.
scenes.animation: Numbers lift and stretch into bars, 200 ms apart.
scenes.narration: Step two: chart. A bar chart is a picture of data where each bar’s height shows a number — here, the millimetres of rain each day. Label the side in equal steps: zero, five, ten, fifteen.
scenes.vids: Keep the card on screen for at least 6 seconds so teachers can read it in a second language.

scenes.visual: A class register open on a teacher’s desk: rows of ticks, with one row showing a gap every fifth column. A teacher’s finger runs along that row and stops; a small thought bubble shows a family at a door.
scenes.animation: Finger slides along the row; the gaps glow teal one by one.
scenes.narration: You already do this with the class register. You tick names every morning. Looking along a pupil’s row, you notice: absent every Friday. Then you decide what to do. Record, spot, decide.
scenes.vids: No pupil names visible; show rows as lines and ticks only.

scenes.visual: Amina Bello pops in beside her class rain table, pointing at one empty box, a sports-day pennant behind her. Three answer cards drop in: a zero, a word card, a question mark with a number.
scenes.animation: Character slides in from the side; answer cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! On sports day, nobody read our rain gauge. What should my pupils write in Wednesday’s box?
scenes.sound: Three gentle ‘pop’ sounds for the cards.
scenes.vids: The app pauses here (diamond marker). For the MP4 shared outside the app, hold this frame for 3 seconds with a small countdown ring.

scenes.visual: The word card gets a blue check badge and slides into the empty box. Then the next day’s row lights up, with a small two-day bracket drawn beside its number.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops (150 ms). Quick 0.8 s confetti of three shapes in kola, sunbird and ink.
scenes.narration: “Missed.” Zero would say no rain fell — and nobody knows that. Thursday’s reading then covers two days, so note that beside the number.
scenes.vids: Use blue for correct (never green) and always pair it with the check icon.

scenes.visual: The class bar chart: two tall bars, then five empty days in a row. A magnifying glass slides over the empty run, which glows teal. Then a rule card appears beside a hand feeling dry soil, and a watering can tips over the tomato bed.
scenes.animation: Magnifier glides in 1 s; the empty run glows; the watering can tips with a small splash.
scenes.narration: Step three: spot the pattern. Here: two wet days, then five dry days in a row. Step four: decide, using a rule the class agreed — say, water if less than five millimetres fell in three days and the soil feels dry. Today, we water.
scenes.vids: Keep the chart simple: no gridlines, bars in teal outline. The rule card shows icons only; add text as an overlay.

scenes.visual: The same garden, now with a probe in the soil. A dotted wireless line runs to a small box on a pole, then to a phone where a table fills and a bar chart grows. A pump beside the bed switches on and waters.
scenes.animation: Dots travel along the line in 1 s; the chart grows bar by bar; the pump starts.
scenes.narration: Connected devices — the Internet of Things — do the same steps automatically. A soil sensor can take a reading every few minutes and send it over a network. A computer stores the readings, draws the chart, and a rule can switch on a pump.
scenes.vids: Generic phone and sensor shapes; no app screens, logos or product designs.

scenes.visual: Okafor in the garden holds a phone showing a big water-drop icon, while the tomato plants beside him droop under a blazing sun. Three answer cards bounce in: a phone with a check, a hand touching soil, a bin.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. Our new garden sensor says the soil is wet. But the tomato leaves are drooping, and it hasn’t rained for five days. What should I do?
scenes.vids: Second diamond marker — the app pauses for the question. In the MP4, hold for 3 seconds, then highlight the hand touching soil.

scenes.visual: The hand-touching-soil card gets the check badge. Okafor crouches, feels dry soil and finds the probe sitting in a damp patch by a dripping tap. Then four summary cards line up: notebook, bar chart, magnifier, watering can.
scenes.animation: Cards line up left to right, 250 ms apart.
scenes.narration: Check before you trust it: feel the soil by the plants and look at the probe — it may sit in a damp spot, or be faulty. Machines help, but people still check. Remember: record, chart, spot the pattern, decide.
scenes.vids: Hold the four cards for 5 seconds.

scenes.visual: Okafor’s classroom. A week of numbers on the board; volunteers draw chalk bars while others check the heights against the table. The class votes on a watering rule with raised hands. End card: Darsi mark and ‘Next: Unit check’.
scenes.animation: Chalk bars grow one by one; end card fades in.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: put a week of rain readings on the board. Pupils draw the bar chart together, find the pattern, and agree a rule for watering the garden.
scenes.sound: Music resolves; no end jingle longer than 1 s.
scenes.vids: Classroom: illustrated pupils in local school uniforms; avoid stereotyped imagery. End card from the Darsi template.

checkpoints.prompt: Nobody read the rain gauge on sports day. What goes in that day’s box?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — “missed” is honest. The next reading then covers two days, so note that beside it.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — 0 claims no rain fell, and a guess isn’t data. Write “missed” so everyone knows.

checkpoints.prompt: The new sensor says “wet”, but the plants droop after five dry days. What first?

options.text: Trust the sensor and don’t water
Feel the soil and check the probe

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — when a reading clashes with what you see, check the soil and the probe before you decide.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — the probe may sit in a damp spot or be faulty. Check the soil and the probe, then decide.

video.vids_prompt: Create a 3-minute animated explainer video for teachers titled “Data in class: record, chart, decide”. Style: flat illustration with bold ink outlines, light grey backgrounds, a tangerine (#ff6a2b) brand colour and a teal (#14b8a6) track accent; no gradients or blur. Main character: Mr Okafor, an enthusiastic Grade 8 science teacher. Follow the script scene by scene: two weeks of rain readings and a garden question; the four data steps; recording in a table; the bar chart; the class-register analogy; a quiz pause; spotting a dry spell and deciding to water; connected devices doing the same steps; a second quiz pause; recap; end with a class chart on the board. Use the narration exactly as written, a warm, calm voice, and keep on-screen text to six words or fewer per scene. No logos or brand names on screen.
